Thyroid nodes: The thyroid lymph nodes are deep anterior cervical lymph nodes found near the thyroid gland on the neck. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyroid_lymph_nodes
Paratracheal cervical nodes: The right and left paratracheal nodes (or paratracheal chains) are groups of lymph nodes located laterally to the trachea; unlike the pretracheal nodes that are located in front of it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paratracheal_lymph_nodes
Jugulodigastric node: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are large lymph nodes of the neck. ==Structure== The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are found in the proximity of where the posterior belly of the digastric muscle crosses the internal jugular vein.
Interpectoral nodes: The small interpectoral lymph nodes are located between the pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles. They receive lymphatic fluid from the muscles and the mammary gland, and deliver lymphatic fluid to the axillary lymphatic plexus. These lymph nodes are susceptible to breast cancer, as the cancer sometimes spreads (metastasizes) to the interpectoral lymph nodes.
Infraclavicular nodes: One or two deltopectoral lymph nodes (or infraclavicular nodes) are found beside the cephalic vein, between the pectoralis major and deltoideus, immediately below the clavicle. They are situated in the course of the external collecting trunks of the arm. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deltopectoral_lymph_nodes
Cubital nodes: One or two lymph nodes along the brachial artery inside the cubital fossa.
Supratrochlear nodes: One or two supratrochlear lymph nodes are placed above the medial epicondyle of the humerus, medial to the basilic vein. Their afferents drain the middle, ring, and little fingers, the medial portion of the hand, and the superficial area over the ulnar side of the forearm; these vessels are, however, in free communication with the other lymphatic vessels of the forearm. Their efferents accompany the basilic vein and join the deeper vessels.
Posterior axillary nodes: A posterior or subscapular group of six or seven glands is placed along the lower margin of the posterior wall of the axilla in the course of the subscapular artery. The afferents of this group drain the skin and muscles of the lower part of the back of the neck and of the posterior thoracic wall; their efferents pass to the central group of axillary glands. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subscapular_axillary_lymph_nodes
Anterior axillary nodes: An anterior or pectoral group consists of four or five glands along the lower border of the Pectoralis minor, in relation with the lateral thoracic artery. Their afferents drain the skin and muscles of the anterior and lateral thoracic walls, and the central and lateral parts of the mamma; their efferents pass partly to the central and partly to the subclavicular groups of axillary glands. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pectoral_axillary_lymph_nodes
Axillary nodes: The axillary lymph nodes or armpit lymph nodes are lymph nodes in the human armpit. Between 20 and 49 in number, they drain lymph vessels from the lateral quadrants of the breast, the superficial lymph vessels from thin walls of the chest and the abdomen above the level of the navel, and the vessels from the upper limb. They are divided in several groups according to their location in the armpit.
Apical axillary nodes: An apical (or medial or subclavicular) group of six to twelve glands is situated partly posterior to the upper portion of the Pectoralis minor and partly above the upper border of this muscle. Its only direct territorial afferents are those that accompany the cephalic vein, and one that drains the upper peripheral part of the mamma. However, it receives the efferents of all the other axillary glands. The efferent vessels of the subclavicular group unite to form the subclavian trunk, which opens either directly into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins or into the jugular lymphatic trunk; on the left side it may end in the thoracic duct.
Central axillary nodes: A central or intermediate group of three or four large glands is imbedded in the adipose tissue near the base of the axilla. Its afferent lymphatic vessels are the efferent vessels of all the preceding groups of axillary glands; its efferents pass to the subclavicular group. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_lymph_nodes
Lateral axillary nodes: A brachial lymph nodes (or lateral group) are group of four to six lymph nodes which lies in relation to the medial and posterior aspects of the axillary vein; the afferents of these glands drain the whole arm with the exception of that portion whose vessels accompany the cephalic vein. The efferent vessels pass partly to the central and subclavicular groups of axillary glands and partly to the inferior deep cervical glands. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachial_lymph_nodes
Abdominal lymph nodes: The lymph nodes of the abdominal cavity are divided into two groups: -the parietal abdominal lymph nodes -and the visceral abdominal lymph nodes
Inferior diaphragmatic nodes: On the inferior surface of diaphragm, near the aortic hiatus. Feneis 306.12
Inferior epigastric nodes: Three or four lymph nodes along the inferior epigastric artery for its territory. Feneis 306.13
Pre-aortic nodes: The preaortic lymph nodes lie in front of the aorta, and may be divided into celiac lymph nodes, superior mesenteric lymph nodes, and inferior mesenteric lymph nodes groups, arranged around the origins of the corresponding arteries. The celiac lymph nodes are grouped into three sets: the gastric, hepatic and splenic lymph nodes. These groups also form their own subgroups. The superior mesenteric lymph nodes are grouped into three sets: the mesenteric, ileocolic and mesocolic lymph nodes.
Lateral aortic nodes: They are located on the left side of the abdominal aorta. Feneis 306.4
Retro-aortic nodes: The retroaortic lymph nodes (or postaortic lymph nodes) are placed below the cisterna chyli, on the bodies of the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae. They receive lymphatic trunks from the lateral and preaortic glands, while their efferents end in the cisterna chyli. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retroaortic_lymph_nodes
Left lumbar nodes: Along the abdominal aorta. Their first function is to be a second relay for the lymph nodes located more caudally. Secondly, they constitute a first relay for the draining of the suprarenal glands, kidneys, ureters, testis, ovaries, uterine tubes, uterine fundus and abdominal wall.
Precaval nodes: They are located in front of the inferior vena cava.
Lateral caval nodes: The lateral caval nodes are located on the right of the inferior vena cava.
Retrocaval nodes: The retrocaval nodes are located behind the inferior vena cava.
Right lumbar nodes: Around the inferior vena cava. Their first function is to be a second relay for the lymph nodes located more caudally. Secondly, they constitute a first relay for the draining of the suprarenal glands, kidneys, ureters, testis, ovaries, uterine tubes, uterine fundus and abdominal wall.
Intermediate lumbar nodes: Between the aorta and the inferior vena cava. Around the inferior vena cava. Their first function is to be a second relay for the lymph nodes located more caudally.
Coeliac nodes: The coeliac nodes are located around the coeliac trunk and are the second filtration relay of the stomach, the duodenum, the liver, the gallbladder, the pancreas and the spleen. They efferent vessels form a part of the intestinal trunk, the others go directly to the chyle cistern.
Right gastric nodes: On the lesser curvature of stomach, they follow the path of the left/right gastric arteries. they drain the stomach and evacuate in the coeliac nodes.
Right gastro-omental nodes: The right and left gastro-omental nodes are located on the great curvature of stomach on the path of the left/right gastro-omental arteries. They drain the stomach and the greater omentum, on the right towards the hepatic nodes, and on the left to the splenic nodes and pancreatic nodes. Feneis 306.18
Splenic nodes: The splenic lymph nodes are found at the splenic hilum and in relation to the tail of the pancreas (pancreaticolienal lymph nodes). Their afferents are derived from the stomach, spleen, and pancreas. The splenic lymph nodes empty into the suprapancreatic, infrapancreatic and omental lymph nodes, which then drain to the coeliac nodes and cisterna chyli.
Visceral abdominal lymph nodes: The visceral abdominal lymph nodes are opposed to the parietal lymph nodes -that are concentrated around the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the main iliac vessels, and the walls of the abdominal cavity. They are linked to each organ of the abdominal cavity: -to the coeliac trunk with -the coeliac nodes
(Suprapyloric node): Above the pyloric part of stomach.
(Subpyloric nodes): On the caudal side of the pyloric part of the stomach.
(Retropyloric nodes): On the dorsal side of the pyloric part of the stomach.
Pyloric nodes: The pyloric lymph nodes are located around the pyloric part of the stomach; they evacuate into the hepatic nodes and the coeliac nodes.
Superior pancreatic nodes: On the superior border of pancreas.
Inferior pancreatic nodes: On the inferior border of pancreas.
Pancreatic nodes: The pancreatic nodes are located on the superior and inferior borders of the pancreas and evacuate partially in the splenic nodes, partially in the mesenteric nodes, and partially in the pancreaticoduodenal nodes. Feneis 306.23
Superior pancreaticoduodenal nodes: Superior part of the pancreaticoduodenal nodes. They evacuate in the hepatic nodes.
Pancreaticoduodenal nodes: Small lymph nodes between the head of pancreas and the duodenum. They drain the pancreas and the duodenum.
Cystic node: Big lympatic node next to the gallbladder. Feneis 306.31
Hepatic nodes: The hepatic lymph nodes consist of the following groups: (a) hepatic, on the stem of the hepatic artery, and extending upward along the common bile duct, between the two layers of the lesser omentum, as far as the porta hepatis; the cystic gland, a member of this group, is placed near the neck of the gall-bladder; (b) subpyloric, four or five in number, in close relation to the bifurcation of the gastroduodenal artery, in the angle between the superior and descending parts of the duodenum; an outlying member of this group is sometimes found above the duodenum on the right gastric (pyloric) artery.
Paracolic superior mesenteric nodes: Those of the superior mesenteric nodes located next to the colon.
Central superior mesenteric nodes: Those of the superior mesenteric nodes located at the trunk of the superior mesenteric artery.
Ileocolic nodes: The ileocolic nodes are located along the ileocolic artery. Evacuation: Coeliac nodes
Precaecal nodes: The precaecal nodes are located along the anterior caecal artery.
Retrocaecal nodes: The retrocaecal are located along the posterior caecal artery.
Appendicular nodes: The appendicular nodes are located along the appendicular artery. They can be missing.
Juxta-intestinal mesenteric nodes: Those of the superior mesenteric nodes located very close to the small intestine.
Middle colic nodes: The left colic nodes follow the path of the left colic artery. The middle colic nodes follow the path of the middle colic artery. The right colic nodes follow the path of the right colic artery.
Right colic nodes: The left colic nodes follow the path of the left colic artery. The middle colic nodes follow the path of the middle colic artery. The right colic nodes follow the path of the right colic artery.
Superior mesenteric nodes: The superior mesenteric lymph nodes may be divided into three principal groups: mesenteric lymph nodes ileocolic lymph nodes mesocolic lymph nodes == Structure ==
Left colic nodes: The left colic nodes follow the path of the left colic artery. The middle colic nodes follow the path of the middle colic artery. The right colic nodes follow the path of the right colic artery.
Sigmoid nodes: Located along the sigmoid artery, for the sigmoid colon and the contiguous colic segment.
Inferior mesenteric nodes: The inferior mesenteric lymph nodes consist of: (a) small glands on the branches of the left colic and sigmoid arteries (b) a group in the sigmoid mesocolon, around the superior hemorrhoidal artery (c) a pararectal group in contact with the muscular coat of the rectum == Structure ==
Pelvic lymph nodes: Located within the pelvis, the pevic lymph nodes are divided between two groups: -the parietal pelvic lymph nodes -and the visceral pelvic lymph nodes
Common iliac nodes: Group of lymph nodes located along the common iliac vessels. They represent the second relay of the lymph nodes of -the pelvic organs, -the genital organs, -the internal wall of the lesser pelvis, -the abdominal wall, -until the umbilicus, -the muscles of the hips and the buttocks. Evacuation: Lumbal lymph nodes and lumbal trunk
Subaortic nodes: Those of the common iliac nodes located beneath the aortic bifurcation, in front of the 4th lumbar vertebra (Vertebra T4).
Medial common iliac nodes: Those of the common iliac nodes located on the medial side of the vascular axis.
Lateral common iliac nodes: Those of the common iliac nodes located on the lateral side of the vascular axis.
Intermediate common iliac nodes: Those of the common iliac nodes located behind the vascular axis, between the medial common iliac nodes and the lateral common iliac nodes.
Median sacral nodes: Those of the commin iliac nodes located in front of the promontory of the sacrum.
External iliac nodes: The external iliac lymph nodes are lymph nodes, from eight to ten in number, that lie along the external iliac vessels. They are arranged in three groups, one on the lateral, another on the medial, and a third on the anterior aspect of the vessels; the third group is, however, sometimes absent. Their principal afferents are derived from the inguinal lymph nodes, the deep lymphatics of the abdominal wall below the umbilicus and of the adductor region of the thigh, and the lymphatics from the glans penis, glans clitoridis, the membranous urethra, the prostate, the fundus of the urinary bladder, the cervix uteri, and upper part of the vagina.
Intermediate external iliac nodes: Group of external iliac nodes located behind the vascular axis, between the medial external iliac nodes and the lateral external iliac nodes.
Internal iliac nodes: The internal iliac lymph nodes (or hypogastric) surround the internal iliac artery and its branches (the hypogastric vessels), and receive the lymphatics corresponding to the distribution of the branches of it, i. e., they receive lymphatics from all the pelvic viscera, from the deeper parts of the perineum, including the membranous and cavernous portions of the urethra, and from the buttock and back of the thigh. The internal iliac lymph nodes also drain the superior half of the rectum, above the pectinate line. It does not receive lymph from the ovary or testis, which drain to the paraaortic lymph nodes.
Lateral sacral nodes: They are located against the sacrum; for the prostate and the neck of uterus.
Inferior gluteal nodes: They are located along the inferior gluteal nodes for the prostate and the proximal part of the ureter.
Superior gluteal nodes: Located along the superior gluteal artery for the wall of the pelvis.
Gluteal nodes: The gluteal nodes are part of the internal iliac nodes, as the lateral sacral nodes. They are divided between the superior gluteal ndoes and the inferior gluteal nodes.
Visceral pelvic lymph nodes: By opposition with the parietal lymph nodes, the visceral lymph nodes are draining only: -the bladder with the paravesical nodes -the uterus with the para-uterine nodes -the vegina with the paravaginal nodes -and the rectum with the pararectal nodes
Paravesical nodes: They are located along the urinary bladder, for the bladder and a part of the prostate.
Prevesical nodes: Those of the vesical nodes located between the urinary bladder and the pubic symphysis.
Postvesical nodes: Those of the paravesical nodes located behind the urinary bladder.
Lymph nodes of lower limb: All the lymph nodes from the inguinal region to the toes: -Inguinal nodes -Superficial inguinal nodes -Deep inguinal nodes -Popliteal nodes -Superficial popliteal nodes -Deep popliteal nodes -Anterior tibial node -Posterior tibial node -Fibular node
Superficial popliteal nodes: The superficial popliteal nodes are located at the proximal extremity of the lesser saphenous vein and drain the lymph of the lateral border of the foot and of the leg. Evacuation: frontwards through the adductor hiatus of the adductor magnus, in the deep inguinal nodes. Feneis 310.25
Popliteal nodes: The popliteal lymph nodes, small in size and some six or seven in number, are embedded in the fat contained in the popliteal fossa, sometimes referred to as the 'knee pit'. One lies immediately beneath the popliteal fascia, near the terminal part of the small saphenous vein, and drains the region from which this vein derives its tributaries, such as superficial regions of the posterolateral aspect of the leg and the plantar aspect of the foot. Another is between the popliteal artery and the posterior surface of the knee-joint.
Inguinal nodes: Inguinal lymph nodes are lymph nodes in the human groin. Located in the femoral triangle of the inguinal region, they are grouped into superficial and deep lymph nodes. The superficial have three divisions: the superomedial, superolateral, and inferior superficial.
Superficial inguinal nodes: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes are the inguinal lymph nodes that form a chain immediately below the inguinal ligament. They lie deep to the fascia of Camper that overlies the femoral vessels at the medial aspect of the thigh. They are bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament in the femoral triangle; laterally by the border of the sartorius muscle, and medially by the adductor longus muscle.
Deep inguinal nodes: There can be three, four or five deep inguinal lymph nodes. They lie medial to the femoral vein under the cribriform fascia. The uppermost node is in the groin, under the inguinal ligament, and is called Cloquet's node (also Rosenmuller's node).
Intrapulmonary nodes: The Intrapulmonary nodes or Lymphatic Vessels of the Lungs originate in two plexuses, a superficial and a deep. The superficial plexus is placed beneath the pulmonary pleura. The deep accompanies the branches of the pulmonary vessels and the ramifications of the bronchi.
Superior diaphragmatic nodes: The superior diaphragmatic lymph nodes lie on the thoracic aspect of the diaphragm, and consist of three sets – anterior, middle, and posterior. The anterior set comprises (a) two or three small nodes behind the base of the xiphoid process, which receive afferents from the convex surface of the liver, and (b) one or two nodes on either side near the junction of the seventh rib with its cartilage, which receive lymphatic vessels from the front part of the diaphragm. The efferent vessels of the anterior set pass to the parasternal lymph nodes.
Prevertebral nodes: The prevertebral lymph nodes are located between the oesophagus and the vertebral column.
Parasternal nodes: The parasternal lymph nodes (or sternal glands) are placed at the anterior ends of the intercostal spaces, by the side of the internal thoracic artery. They derive afferents from the mamma; from the deeper structures of the anterior abdominal wall above the level of the umbilicus; from the upper surface of the liver through a small group of glands which lie behind the xiphoid process; and from the deeper parts of the anterior portion of the thoracic wall. Their efferents usually unite to form a single trunk on either side; this may open directly into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins, or that of the right side may join the right subclavian trunk, and that of the left…
Intercostal nodes: The intercostal lymph nodes (intercostal glands) occupy the posterior parts of the intercostal spaces, in relation to the intercostal vessels. They receive the deep lymphatics from the postero-lateral aspect of the chest; some of these vessels are interrupted by small lateral intercostal glands. The efferents of the glands in the lower four or five spaces unite to form a trunk, which descends and opens either into the cisterna chyli or into the commencement of the thoracic duct.
Prepericardial nodes: Located between the sternum and the pericardium, the prepericardial nodes drain the sternum and the anterior part of the pericardium. Evacuation: Parasternal nodes
Mediastinal lymph nodes: Mediastinal lymph nodes are lymph nodes located in the mediastinum. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediastinal_lymph_node
Juxta-oesophageal nodes: They are located next to the oesophagus but belong to the lungs.
Brachiocephalic nodes: In front of the aortic arch and of its branches; along the brachiocephalic veins. They drain the thymus, the thyroid, the pericardium, the parasternal nodes. Evacuation: -left broncho-mediastinal lymphatic trunk -right broncho-mediastinal lymphatic trunk
Lymph node: A lymph node, or lymph gland, is a kidney-shaped organ of the lymphatic system, and the adaptive immune system. A large number of lymph nodes are linked throughout the body by the lymphatic vessels. They are major sites of lymphocytes that include B and T cells.
Regions of head: The cranial region encompasses the upper part of the head while the facial region encompasses the lower half of the head beginning below the ears. The forehead is referred to as the frontal region. The eyes are referred to as the orbital or ocular region. The cheeks are referred to as the buccal region. The ears are referred to as the auricle or otic region. The nose is referred to as the nasal region. The mouth is referred to as the oral region. The chin is referred to as the mental region. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_human_anatomical_regions
Regions of epicranium: The Epicranium is the medical term for the collection of structures covering the cranium. It consists of the muscles, aponeurosis, and skin. These are its regions:
Eyebrow: An eyebrow is an area of short hairs above each eye that follows the shape of the lower margin of the brow ridges of some mammals. In humans, eyebrows serve two main functions: first, communication through facial expression, and second, prevention of sweat, water, and other debris from falling down into the eye socket. It is common for people to modify their eyebrows by means of hair removal and makeup.
Mastoid region: Behind the ear. See: Mastoid process
Occipital region: Back of the head. See: Occipital bone, occiput
Parietal region: Postero-superior part of the head, between the frontal region, the occipital region, and the two temporal regions.
Temporal region: Above and around the ear. See: Temple
Cavity of concha: Concha is the hollow next to the ear canal.
Concha of auricle: Concha is the hollow next to the ear canal.
Cymba conchae: Cymba conchae is the narrowest end of the concha.
Anterior notch of auricle: Incisure between the tragus and the crura of antihelix.
Antihelix: Arciform relief of the auricle located in front the posterior part of the helix
Antitragus: It is a small tubercle on the visible part of the ear, the pinna. The antitragus is located just above the earlobe and points anteriorly. It is separated from the tragus by the intertragic notch.
Auricular region: The ears are referred to as the auricular region, or otic region. See: ear, external ear
Crura of antihelix: Each of the two upper divisions of the antihelix, surrounding the triangular fossa.
Fossa antihelica: Depression at the posterior surface of the auricular cartilage, corresponding to the root of the helix on the anterior surface.
Helix: External curvy border of the auricle
Intertragic incisure: Notch between the tragus and the antitragus.
Lobule of auricle: Inferior extremity of the auricle, without cartilage.
Scapha: The depression or groove between the helix and the antihelix.
Tragus: The tragus is a small pointed eminence of the external ear, situated in front of the concha, and projecting backward over the meatus. It also is the name of hair growing at the entrance of the ear. Its name comes the Ancient Greek tragos (τράγος), meaning 'goat', and is descriptive of its general covering on its under surface with a tuft of hair, resembling a goat's beard.
Triangular fossa: Antero-superior depression between the two branches of the antihelix (crura of antihelix).
Posterior auricular groove: Shallow depression between the antitragus and the antihelix.
Orbital region: The eyes are referred to as the orbital region (or ocular region) See: Orbit
Upper eyelid: An eyelid is a thin fold of skin that covers and protects an eye. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle retracts the eyelid, exposing the cornea to the outside, giving vision. This can be either voluntarily or involuntarily.
Lower eyelid: An eyelid is a thin fold of skin that covers and protects an eye. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle retracts the eyelid, exposing the cornea to the outside, giving vision. This can be either voluntarily or involuntarily.
Eyelids: An eyelid is a thin fold of skin that covers and protects an eye. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle retracts the eyelid, exposing the cornea to the outside, giving vision. This can be either voluntarily or involuntarily.
Nasal region: The nose is referred to as the nasal region.
External nose: The human nose is the most protruding part of the face. It bears the nostrils and is the first organ of the respiratory system. It is also the principal organ in the olfactory system.
Root of nose: The nasal root is the top of the nose that attaches the nose to the forehead. The nasal root is above the bridge and below the glabella, forming an indentation known as the nasion at the frontonasal suture where the frontal bone meets the nasal bones. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_nose
Apex of nose: Anterior extremity of the nose. See: Nasal region; nose
Oral region: The mouth is referred to as the oral region; it is one of the regions of the face. Several structures are parts of the oral region: -Philtrum -Tubercle of upper lip -Labial commissure -Angle of mouth
Labial commissure: The commissure is the corner of the mouth, where the vermillion border of the superior labium (upper lip) meets that of the inferior labium (lower lip). The commissure is important in facial appearance, particularly during some functions, including smiling. As such it is of interest to dental surgeons. Diseases that involve the commissure include angular chelitis.
Philtrum: The philtrum (Latin: philtrum from Ancient Greek φίλτρον phíltron, lit. "love charm"), or medial cleft, is a vertical indentation in the middle area of the upper lip, common to therian mammals, extending in humans from the nasal septum to the tubercle of the upper lip. Together with a glandular rhinarium and slit-like nostrils, it is believed to constitute the primitive condition for at least therian mammals. Monotremes lack a philtrum, though this could be due to the specialised, beak-like jaws in living species.
Tubercle of upper lip: Small elevation on the upper lip, at the extremity of the philtrum.
Upper lip: Lips are a visible body part at the mouth of many animals, including humans. Lips are soft, movable, and serve as the opening for food intake and in the articulation of sound and speech. Human lips are a tactile sensory organ, and can be an erogenous zone when used in kissing and other acts of intimacy.
Buccal region: The cheeks are referred to as the buccal region.
Cheek: The cheeks (Latin: buccae) constitute the area of the face below the eyes and between the nose and the left or right ear. "Buccal" means relating to the cheek. In humans, the region is innervated by the buccal nerve. The area between the inside of the cheek and the teeth and gums is called the vestibule or buccal pouch or buccal cavity and forms part of the mouth.
Mental region: The chin is referred to as the mental region. See: Mental protuberance, Mandible, Gnathion
Chin: The human chin is the forward pointed part of the anterior mandible (mental region) below the lower lip. A fully developed human skull has a chin of between 0.7 cm and 1.1 cm. == Evolution ==
Mentolabial sulcus: Depression between the lower lip and the chin.
Zygomatic region: Above the buccal region and the parotid region. It corresponds to the zygomatic bone and the zygomatic arch.
Nasolabial sulcus: Groove from the ala of nose to the angle of mouth. See: Oral region
Regions of face: The facial region encompasses the lower half of the head beginning below the ears: -Orbital region -Infra-orbital region -Buccal region -Parotideomasseteric region -Zygomatic region -Nasal region -Nasolabial sulcus -Oral region -Mentolabial sulcus -Mental region
Posterior region of neck: Covers the ascending part of trapezius muscle.
Regions of neck: Beneath the regions of head, above the regions of thorax and the regions of back. -Anterior region of neck -Sternocleidomastoid region -Lateral region of neck -Posterior region of neck
Lateral region of neck: By opposition to the anterior region of neck, the posterior region of neck, and the sternocleidomastoid region. The lateral region of neck includes: -the greater supraclavicular fossa -the omoclavicular triangle -the occipital triangle
Submandibular triangle: The submandibular triangle (or submaxillary or digastric triangle) corresponds to the region of the neck immediately beneath the body of the mandible. == Boundaries and coverings == It is bounded:
Submental triangle: The submental triangle (or suprahyoid triangle) is a division of the anterior triangle of the neck. == Boundaries == It is limited to:
Suprahyoid region: Horizontal part of the neck, beneath the mandible. The suprahyoid region is divided between the submandibular triangle and the submental triangle.
Carotid triangle: The carotid triangle (or superior carotid triangle) is a portion of the anterior triangle of the neck. == Coverings and boundaries == It is bounded:
Muscular triangle: The inferior carotid triangle (or muscular triangle), is bounded, in front, by the median line of the neck from the hyoid bone to the sternum; behind, by the anterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid; above, by the superior belly of the omohyoid. It is covered by the integument, superficial fascia, platysma, and deep fascia, ramifying in which are some of the branches of the supraclavicular nerves. Beneath these superficial structures are the sternohyoid and sternothyroid, which, together with the anterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, conceal the lower part of the common carotid artery. This vessel is enclosed within its sheath, together with the internal jugular vein and vagus…
Infrahyoid region: Part of the anterior regions of the neck located beneath the hyoid bone. It includes the carotid triangle and the muscular triangle.
Sternocleidomastoid region: It corresponds to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Lesser supraclavicular fossa: The lesser supraclavicular fossa is a palpable just next to the jugular notch; it is located between the sternal and the clavicular head of sternocleidomastoid muscle. It is The Supraclavicular fossa is an indentation (fossa) immediately above the clavicle. It is divided into the greater supraclavicular fossa and the lesser supraclavicular fossa.
Epigastric region: In anatomy, the epigastrium (or epigastric region) is the upper central region of the abdomen. It is located between the costal margins and the subcostal plane. Pain may be referred to the epigastrium from damage to structures derived from the foregut.
Umbilical region: The umbilical region, is one of the nine regions of the abdomen. It is the region that surrounds the area around the umbilicus and is placed approximately half way between the xiphoid process and the pubic symphysis. This region of the abdomen contains part of the stomach, the head of the pancreas, the duodenum, a section of the transverse colon and the lower aspects of the left and right kidney.
Umbilicus: The umbilicus is a prominent scar on the abdomen, with its position being relatively consistent among humans. The skin around the waist at the level of the umbilicus is supplied by the tenth thoracic spinal nerve (T10 dermatome). The umbilicus itself typically lies at a vertical level corresponding to the junction between the L3 and L4 vertebrae, with a normal variation among people between the L3 and L5 vertebrae.
Hypochondriac region: In anatomy, the division of the abdomen into regions can employ a nine-region scheme. The hypochondrium refers to the two hypochondriac regions in the upper third of the abdomen; the left hypochondrium and right hypochondrium. They are located on the lateral sides of the abdominal wall respectively, inferior to (below) the thoracic cage, being separated by the epigastrium.
Hypogastric region: The hypogastrium (also called the hypogastric region or suprapubic region) is a region of the abdomen located below the umbilical region. The pubis bone constitutes its lower limit. The roots of the word hypogastrium mean "below the stomach"; the roots of suprapubic mean "above the pubic bone".
Inguinal region: /GROIN In human anatomy, the groin (the adjective is inguinal, as in inguinal canal) is the junctional area (also known as the inguinal region) between the abdomen and the thigh on either side of the pubic bone. This is also known as the medial compartment of the thigh that consists of the adductor muscles of the hip or the groin muscles.
Lateral region of abdomen: Region located laterally to the medioclavicular line, between the subcostal plane and the supracristal crest.
Regions of abdomen: The human abdomen is divided into quadrants and regions by anatomists and physicians for the purposes of study, diagnosis, and treatment. The division into four quadrants allows the localisation of pain and tenderness, scars, lumps, and other items of interest, narrowing in on which organs and tissues may be involved. The quadrants are referred to as the left lower quadrant, left upper quadrant, right upper quadrant and right lower quadrant.
Lumbar region: In tetrapod anatomy, lumbar is an adjective that means of or pertaining to the abdominal segment of the torso, between the diaphragm and the sacrum. The lumbar region is sometimes referred to as the lower spine, or as an area of the back in its proximity. In human anatomy the five lumbar vertebrae (vertebrae in the lumbar region of the back) are the largest and strongest in the movable part of the spinal column, and can be distinguished by the absence of a foramen in the transverse process, and by the absence of facets on the sides of the body.
Infrascapular region: Between the scapular region and the lumbar region.
Triangle of auscultation: The triangle of auscultation is a relative thinning of the musculature of the back, situated along the medial border of the scapula which allows for improved listening to the lungs. == Boundaries == It has the following boundaries:
Regions of back: Posterior region of the trunk, including: -Vertebral region -Scapular region -Triangle of auscultation -Infrascapular region -Lumbar region -Sacral region -Coccygeal region
Anal region: Region around the anus, limited in front by a line passing by the two ischiatic tuberosities.
Urogenital region: Part of the perineal region in front of the line passing by the two ischiatic tuberosities.
Regions of perineum: The perineal region includes the urogenital region and the anal region.
Regions of upper limb: These regions are: -the axillary region -the deltoid region -the brachial region -the cubital region -the antebrachial region -the carpal region -the regions of hand
Medial bicipital groove: The medial bicipital groove is seen on the surface anatomy of the upper arm. It is formed by the longitudinal hollow between the biceps and triceps muscles. The pulse of the brachial artery can be felt in the medial bicipital groove.It should be distinguished from the bicipital groove or intertubercular sulcus, which is not a surface anatomy structure. It is the groove where the long head of biceps tendon runs between the greater and lesser tubercles below the humeral head before inserting into the superior glenoid rim. The lateral bicipital groove is seen on the lateral aspect of the upper arm, and is formed by the same anatomical structures as the medial groove.
Palm: Palm most commonly refers to: Palm of the hand, the central region of the front of the hand Palm trees, of family Arecaceae List of Arecaceae genera Several other plants known as "palm"Palm or Palms may also refer to: == Music ==
Cubital fossa: The cubital fossa, chelidon, or elbow pit, is the triangular area on the anterior side of the upper limb between the arm and forearm of a human or other hominid animals. It lies anteriorly to the elbow (Latin cubitus) when in standard anatomical position. == Boundaries ==
Femoral triangle: The femoral triangle (or Scarpa's triangle) is an anatomical region of the upper third of the thigh. It is a subfascial space which appears as a triangular depression below the inguinal ligament when the thigh is flexed, abducted and laterally rotated. == Structure ==
Popliteal fossa: The popliteal fossa (sometimes referred to as hough,[1] or kneepit in analogy to the cubital fossa) is a shallow depression located at the back of the knee joint. The bones of the popliteal fossa are the femur and the tibia. Like other flexion surfaces of large joints (groin, armpit, cubital fossa and essentially the anterior part of the neck), it is an area where blood vessels and nerves pass relatively superficially, and with an increased number of lymph nodes.
Lateral region of thorax: Region lateral to the mammary and inframammary regions
Regions of thorax: Anterior and lateral parts of the thorax; the posterior part is part of the regions of the back. Several parts are described within the regions of thorax: -the anterior region of thorax -the lateral region of thorax
Pectoral region: The pectoral region includes the mammary region and the inframammary region.
Mammary region: From 'Breast': The breast is one of two prominences located on the upper ventral region of a primate's torso. Both females and males develop breasts from the same embryological tissues.
Infraclavicular fossa: The Infraclavicular fossa is an indentation, or fossa, immediately below the clavicle, above the third rib and between the deltoid muscle laterally and medioclavicular line medially. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infraclavicular_fossa
Presternal region: The presternal region corresponds to the sternum.
Deltopectoral triangle: Triangle between the clavicle, the deltoid muscle and the pectoralis major muscle.
Anterior region of thorax: The anterior region of thorax is a part of the regions of thorax, as the lateral region of thorax. The anterior region of thorax includes: -Precordium -Presternal region -Infraclavicular fossa -Deltopectoral triangle -Deltopectoral groove -Pectoral region
Eyelashes: An eyelash (also called lash) (Latin: Cilia) is one of the hairs that grows at the edge of the eyelids. It grows in one layer on the edge of the upper and lower eyelids. Eyelashes protect the eye from debris, dust and small particles and perform some of the same functions as whiskers do on a cat or a mouse in the sense that they are sensitive to being touched, thus providing a warning that an object (such as an insect) is near the eye (which then closes reflexively).
Hairs: Hair is a protein filament that grows from follicles found in the dermis. Hair is one of the defining characteristics of mammals. The human body, apart from areas of glabrous skin, is covered in follicles which produce thick terminal and fine vellus hair.
Distal: Located in the direction opposed to the trunk. Feneis 4.37
Dorsal: On the side of the back. Feneis 4.15
Fibular: Related to the fibula; located on the side of the fibula. Feneis 4.42
Plantar: Related to the sole of the foot. Feneis 4.45
Proximal: Located in the direction of the trunk. Feneis 4.36
Radial: Located on the side of the radius. Feneis 4.40
Tibial: Related to the tibia; located on the tibia's side of the leg
Ulnar: Related to the ulna. Located on the side of the ulna. Feneis 4.41
Ventral: On the side of the belly. Feneis 4.14
Transverse planes: The transverse plane or axial plane (also called the horizontal plane or transaxial plane) is an imaginary plane that divides the body into superior and inferior parts. It is perpendicular to the coronal plane and sagittal plane. It is one of the planes of the body used to describe the location of body parts in relation to each other. == List of clinically relevant anatomical planes ==
Mamillary line: Can be at the same place as the mediocalvicular line. Feneis 4.53
Midclavicular line: Vertical line passing through the middle of the clavicle. Feneis 4.52
Parasternal line: Vertical line at equal distance between the sternal and midclavicular lines. Feneis 4.51
Sternal line: Located at the lateral border of the sternum. Feneis 4.50
Abduction: Abduction is a motion that pulls a structure or part away from the midline of the body, carried out by one or more abductor muscles. In the case of fingers and toes, it is spreading the digits apart, away from the centerline of the hand or foot. For example, raising the arms up, such as when tightrope-walking, is an example of abduction at the shoulder.
Adduction: Adduction is a motion that pulls a structure or part towards the midline of the body, or towards the midline of a limb, carried out by one or more adductor muscles. In the case of fingers and toes, it is bringing the digits together, towards the centerline of the hand or foot. Dropping the arms to the sides, and bringing the knees together, are examples of adduction.
Circumduction: Circumduction is a conical movement of a body part, such as a ball and socket joint or the eye. Circumduction is a combination of flexion, extension, adduction and abduction. Circumduction can be best performed at ball and socket joints, such as the hip and shoulder, but may also be performed by other parts of the body such as fingers, hands, feet, and head.
Lateral rotation: External rotation (lateral rotation or extorsion) is rotation (of the front part) away from the center of the body.
Medial rotation: Internal rotation (medial rotation or intorsion) is rotation (of the front part of the body) towards the axis of the body.
Anterior median line: Median line in the median plane of the trunk. Feneis 4.49
Posterior median line: Median vertical line at the back of the trunk. Feneis 4.58
Paravertebral line: Vertical line passing by the top of the transverse processes, determined only by the radiological examination. Feneis 4.58
Scapular line: Vertical line passing through the inferior angle of the scapula. Feneis 4.57
Anterior axillary line: Located at the level of the anterior axillary fold. Feneis 4.54
Posterior axillary line: Located at the level of the posterior axillary fold. Feneis 4.56
Frontal: Belonging to the forehead; in a plane parallel to the forehead. Feneis 4.16
Occipital: Belonging to the occiput; on the side of the occiput. Feneis 4.17
Cranial: Belonging to the head; in the direction of the head. Feneis 4.20
Caudal: In the direction opposite to the head. Feneis 4.21
Supination: Supination of the forearm occurs when the forearm or palm are rotated outwards. As an example, when a person is typing on a computer keyboard, their hands are pronated; when washing their face, they are supinated.
Pronation: Pronation at the forearm is a rotational movement where the hand and upper arm are turned so the thumbs point towards the body. When the forearm and hand are supinated, the thumbs point away from the body. As an example, when a person is typing on a computer keyboard, their hands are pronated; when washing their face, they are supinated.
Palmar: Related to the palm; located on its side. Volar, volaris: Synonyme of palmar Feneis 4.44
Inversion: Inversion is the movement of the sole towards the median plane. For example, inversion describes the motion when an ankle is twisted.
Eversion: Eversion is the movement of the sole of the foot away from the median plane.
Plantar flexion: Plantar flexion or plantarflexion is the movement which decreases the angle between the sole of the foot and the back of the leg; for example, the movement when depressing a car pedal or standing on tiptoes. Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion refer to extension or flexion of the foot at the ankle. These terms refer to flexion in direction of the "back" of the foot, which is the upper surface of the foot when standing, and flexion in direction of the sole of the foot.
Dorsiflexion: Dorsiflexion is where the toes are brought closer to the shin. This decreases the angle between the dorsum of the foot and the leg. For example, when walking on the heels the ankle is described as being in dorsiflexion.
Coronal planes: A coronal plane (also known as the frontal plane) is any vertical plane that divides the body into ventral and dorsal (belly and back) sections. It is one of the three main planes of the body used to describe the location of body parts in relation to each other axis. == Details ==
Paramedian plane: The term parasagittal is used to describe any plane parallel or adjacent to a given sagittal plane. Specific named parasagittal planes include: The midclavicular line crosses through the clavicle. Lateral sternal and parasternal planes. The term sagittal is derived from the Latin word 'sagitta', meaning 'arrow'.
Median plane: The median plane also called a mid-sagittal plane is used to describe the sagittal plane as it bisects the body vertically through the midline marked by the navel, dividing the body exactly in left and right side. The term parasagittal plane is used to refer to any plane parallel to the sagittal and median plane. It is one of the lines used to define the right upper quadrant of the human abdomen.
